## A Manifesto That Must Compile

On March 9, 1993, Eric Hughes circulated “A Cypherpunk's Manifesto.” Its opening formulation made a fundamental distinction: privacy is necessary for an open society; privacy is not secrecy; it is the power to reveal oneself selectively to the world (Hughes, 1993). Secrecy seeks to conceal a fact entirely, whereas privacy governs the relationship among contexts and audiences. A person may tell a physician one thing, a friend another, and the state a third—and preserve autonomy precisely because these disclosures cannot be reduced to a single dossier.

The manifesto's second formulation became the movement's program: “Cypherpunks write code.” A political demand had to be embodied in working anonymous remailers, digital signatures, electronic cash, and encryption tools. This distinguished the cypherpunks from a purely legal defense of privacy. Law may prohibit data collection, but electronic communication makes copying and combining records too easy; each party's knowledge must therefore be constrained technically to what a particular transaction requires.

## From a Shared Secret to a Public Key

Classical symmetric cryptography presumes a shared secret key. This is effective when the parties already possess a secure channel over which to exchange the key, but it scales poorly in an open network of strangers. In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman established new directions in cryptography: a method for agreeing on a secret over a public channel and the idea of a digital signature based on separate public and private keys (Diffie & Hellman, 1976).

The conceptual revolution was not merely a stronger cipher. The architecture of trust changed. Participants could establish a confidential channel without a previously shared secret, while a signature made it possible to verify the origin and integrity of a message without acquiring the ability to forge it. Mathematical asymmetry produced a social asymmetry of authority: verification became public while the creation of proof remained private.

David Chaum extended this principle to transactional systems. In “Security without Identification,” he warned of a “dossier society” in which linked records could reveal a person's lifestyle, location, and relationships (Chaum, 1985). His proposals for blind signatures and separate pseudonyms demonstrated that a system could verify an entitlement or payment without learning a persistent identity. This was an early formulation of data minimization: organizational security and user privacy need not form a zero-sum relationship.

In 1991, Phil Zimmermann released Pretty Good Privacy, making strong email encryption available to owners of personal computers. In “Why I Wrote PGP,” he connected the program to the spread of electronic surveillance and the ordinary person's right to use the envelope of the digital age (Zimmermann, 1991/1999). PGP combined cryptographic primitives with a user-facing product and a “web of trust,” in which keys are certified not by a single center but by participants' signatures.

## The Community of 1992

The first gathering of the future cypherpunks took place in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1992; its organizers included Hughes, Timothy May, and John Gilmore. On September 21, Hughes welcomed the participants to an already functioning mailing list and thanked Gilmore for hosting the server (Hughes, 1992). The community itself existed as networked text: program code, technical disputes, political philosophy, and experiments circulated through the very channel its members sought to protect.

Timothy May described the more radical horizon of “crypto anarchy”: strong encryption and anonymous markets would weaken the ability of states to control information and transactions (May, 1988/1992). Hughes was more institutionally nuanced. His manifesto acknowledged that privacy extends only as far as one's fellows cooperate; privacy on a mass scale must be part of a social contract. Code is therefore necessary but not self-sufficient.

## The First Crypto War

The political context made this program contentious. In the United States, strong cryptography was long regulated as military technology, and the export of software was restricted. On April 16, 1993, the Clinton administration announced the Clipper Chip initiative: government-approved encryption would use a key-escrow system allowing authorized agencies to obtain access to content (White House, 1993). For the government, this was a compromise between confidentiality and lawful interception; for critics, it was a centralized vulnerability and a presumption that private communication should remain accessible to the state.

The dispute demonstrated that a “back door” is not a policy external to mathematics. It changes the threat model and the distribution of keys—that is, the architecture of security itself. Universal reserve access for a “good” party creates a mechanism that may be implemented incorrectly, stolen, or expanded beyond its original purpose.

In 1995, the Electronic Frontier Foundation filed suit on behalf of mathematician Daniel Bernstein against the export restrictions. Bernstein wanted to publish an algorithm, a scholarly description, and source code; the government regime required permission, effectively treating publication as the export of a weapon. *Bernstein v. U.S. Department of Justice* became a key case in the recognition of source code as a form of expression protected by the First Amendment and contributed to the liberalization of the rules (EFF, 1995–2000). The formula “code is speech” connected mathematical publication, software functionality, and constitutional law.

## What Mathematics Can Actually Guarantee

The title “privacy is mathematics” expresses the cypherpunk shift from a promise to a verifiable property. If an algorithm is open, its assumptions are explicit, the key is sufficiently strong, and the implementation is correct, confidentiality does not depend on the goodwill of the channel's operator. Ciphertext can pass through hostile infrastructure; security rests on computational difficulty rather than secrecy of design.

Mathematics, however, guarantees only the property formalized in the model. It does not automatically conceal metadata—who communicated with whom, or when. It does not protect plaintext on a compromised endpoint. It does not prevent coercion of the key holder, an interface error, a weak password, or centralized certificate issuance. It does not decide which data a system should collect in the first place, and it does not provide equal access to secure tools.

Even end-to-end encryption can coexist with extensive behavioral profiling. A system may be unable to read a message's content while knowing the social graph, location, frequency of contacts, and device characteristics. Chaum's analysis remains broader than message encryption: privacy requires the transaction to be designed so that it does not create unnecessary linkability.

## Protocol as Constitution

The cypherpunks recognized something that political theory often left to engineers: an architecture of communication distributes rights before any court does. If a system stores a master key, it contains a sovereign of exception; if a link is public by default, secrecy requires an additional act; if an identifier is persistent, combining contexts becomes inexpensive. A protocol is not a society's complete law, but it is part of its effective constitution.

The opposition between “mathematics instead of politics” is nevertheless false. The choice of algorithm, the standard, funding for audits, the availability of implementations, liability for breaches, and the limits of state intervention remain political decisions. Hughes is more precise than his own slogan: privacy requires both code and cooperation. Mathematics can make a violation costly and verifiable; society must decide where, and for whom, such protection will be the norm.
